Hi Aria —

Short answer up front: a hybrid-first approach. Rough starting point (subject to perf validation):
- L4: 40 slots (primary for embeddings, short-form generation, most of the tail)
- A100 (80GB): 10 slots (medium context, batched generative workloads)
- H100 (80GB or 94GB): 2–4 slots (reserved for long-context summarization and latency-critical flows)

Rationale / tradeoffs:
- L4: best price/per-token for small-context generation and embeddings. Excellent for high QPS and cheap caching. Not ideal for >16k context without chunking.
- A100: good middle ground; strong throughput with larger memory for KV cache. Better when you can batch and accept slightly higher latency.
- H100: higher single-request throughput for heavy attention workloads and large contexts, stronger fp16/fp8 perf and memory bandwidth. Use for workloads where you can't shard the KV cache easily and where accuracy of FP16->FP8 conversions matters.

Ops notes:
- KV cache sizing matters: long-context flows will consume a lot of per-request KV. We recommend reserving H100 with pinned KV cache for the 64k flows so you avoid cold cache evictions.
- Quantization: L4 runs int8/4-bit well; A100/H100 we recommend 4-bit quantization for most gen tasks but run evals against your top-20 prompts to validate generation quality.
- Batching: L4 is latency-friendly for small batch sizes; A100 yields big wins at higher batch sizes. H100 shines for single-shot long-context performance.
- Fallthrough strategy: if H100 isn't available, we can route long-context requests to A100 with a degraded SLA (latency increase + incremental cost). For summaries that absolutely require H100-level latency/quality, implement a graceful degrade to chunked summarization via L4 + a reassembly step.

I'll drop a matching benchmark matrix (A100 vs H100 vs L4 across your typical prompt set) and a conservative slotting plan for the SOW. Lauren, can you add the commercial/term constraints we discussed? Dev — please add ops constraints for pinned KV caches and burst routing.

—Karthik

Quick ops-addendum:

1) Scheduling & preemption: if Nimbus signs Reserved capacity but requests burst, we'll prefer a two-pool config: one reserved (A100/H100) and one shared burst (L4 + spot A100 capacity). Avoid preemption for H100 reserved pools to protect latency SLAs.

2) Slot granularity: for long-context summarization we should allocate whole-device slots (no tiling) to avoid cross-tenant KV thrash. That means 1 H100 slot per concurrent long-context session.

3) Autoscale policy suggestion: scale L4 by QPS with fast scale-up/scale-down (cold-starts are cheap); autoscale A100 by token backlog windows; H100 by manual or canary triggers (to avoid noisy scaling).

4) Observability: expose per-slot KV hit-rate, average chronic eviction counts, and per-request inferred memory usage so we can surface pressure early.

I'll attach the microbench run for multi-session long-context on H100 and A100 — numbers in the spreadsheet Karthik referenced.

Aria / Ethan —

Appended a concise plan and runbook link for inclusion in the SOW. Summary:
- Initial committed mix (conservative): 30 L4 / 8 A100 / 3 H100 (we pushed H100 +1 from prior based on your long-context tail)
- Reserved vs burst: reserve 75% of compute for A100/H100 (latency and KV stability), leave L4 primarily as burstable reserved/burst pool to optimize cost.
- Fallthrough: explicit SLA tiering in SOW:
  - Tier 1 (SLA-covered): served on H100 or reserved A100 with <200ms additional latency target.
  - Tier 2 (degraded): routed to A100 (if H100 exhausted) with capped latency increase and explicit per-token surcharge (we estimate ~18% higher cost).
  - Tier 3 (fallback): chunk + reassemble on L4 for non-blocking completion when both H100/A100 capacity constrained.
